questions.question: Ravi has a square piece of poster board with an area of 1 m². He folds it into 2 equal rows and colours 1 whole row red. Then he folds it into 4 equal columns and colours 3 whole columns blue. The folds make 8 equal small rectangles, and exactly 3 of them are coloured both red and blue. What is 1/2 × 3/4, the double-coloured part of the board?
questions.explain: The double-coloured part is 3 of the 8 equal rectangles, which is exactly numerator × numerator over denominator × denominator: (1 × 3)/(2 × 4) = 3/8. The trap is giving the fractions a common denominator first — 2/4 × 3/4 = 6/4 is bigger than the whole board.

questions.question: Mia's tray of banana bread counts as 1 whole. She cuts it into 3 equal rows and glazes 2 whole rows. She also cuts it into 6 equal columns and puts seeds on 5 whole columns. The cuts make 18 equal pieces, and 10 of those pieces are both glazed and seeded. Written in lowest terms, what fraction of the tray is both glazed and seeded?
questions.explain: Multiply straight across: (2 × 5)/(3 × 6) = 10/18, which is the 10 double-marked pieces out of all 18, and 10/18 in lowest terms is 5/9. The trap is switching to a common denominator first — 4/6 × 5/6 = 20/6 is more than the whole tray.

questions.question: A 1 m² square of grid paper is split into 4 equal columns and 3 equal rows, making 12 equal small squares. A garden bed is drawn on it as a rectangle 3/4 m wide (3 of the 4 columns) and 2/3 m tall (2 of the 3 rows), so it covers 6 of the small squares. What is the area of the garden bed?
questions.explain: Area is length × width: (3 × 2)/(4 × 3) = 6/12 = 1/2 m², which matches the 6 covered squares out of 12. The trap is adding the side lengths instead of multiplying — 3/4 + 2/3 = 1 5/12 m² is larger than the whole square of paper.

questions.question: A chocolate bar counts as 1 whole. It is scored into 3 equal columns and 4 equal rows, making 12 equal squares. Sam has 2 of the 3 columns left, and he eats 1 of the 4 rows of those leftover columns — that is 2 of the 12 squares. What fraction of the whole bar did Sam eat?
questions.explain: He ate 1/4 of the 2/3 that was left: (1 × 2)/(4 × 3) = 2/12 = 1/6 of the whole bar, the 2 squares out of all 12. The trap is comparing those 2 squares only to the 8 squares that were left over, which answers a different question.

questions.question: Leo is making 3 banners for the school gym, and each banner needs 2 1/4 m of ribbon. How much ribbon does he need altogether?
questions.explain: Change the mixed number to an improper fraction first: 2 1/4 = 9/4, and 9/4 × 3 = 27/4 = 6 3/4 m. The trap is multiplying only the whole number and carrying the 1/4 along to get 6 1/4 m — each of the 3 banners needs that quarter metre too.

questions.question: Kai works out 2/5 × 3/10 by multiplying numerator × numerator and denominator × denominator, then writing the answer in lowest terms. Which answer should he get?
questions.explain: Multiply straight across: (2 × 3)/(5 × 10) = 6/50, and 6/50 in lowest terms is 3/25. The trap is making a common denominator first — that is a step for adding, and 4/10 × 3/10 gives 1 1/5, which is bigger than both fractions you started with.

questions.question: Nadia has 5/6 of a litre of milk in a bottle and pours 1/2 of that milk into a jug. How many litres go into the jug?
questions.explain: Half of 5/6 is (1 × 5)/(2 × 6) = 5/12 L. The trap is rewriting 1/2 as 3/6 to get a common denominator first, which gives 2 1/2 L — more milk than the bottle ever held, and taking part of an amount must make it smaller.

questions.question: Ben has a board 1 1/2 m long and cuts off 3/4 of it to make a shelf. How long is the shelf?
questions.explain: Write 1 1/2 as the improper fraction 3/2, then (3 × 3)/(2 × 4) = 9/8 = 1 1/8 m. The trap is keeping the whole number 1 and multiplying only the fraction parts, which gives 1 3/8 m — the whole number has to be multiplied as well.

questions.question: A hoodie at the school store normally costs $36. This week it is marked down to 2/3 of that price, and Emma also has a coupon that brings the marked price down to 3/4 of it. How much does Emma pay?
questions.explain: Do the two steps in order: 2/3 of $36 is $24, then 3/4 of $24 is $18 — or multiply 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2 first and take half of $36. The trap is stopping after the first step at $24, or adding the two fractions, which makes the hoodie cost more than it did at the start.

questions.question: Owen is building a fence from 4 sections that are each 3 1/2 m long. He writes 3 × 4 = 12, keeps the 1/2, and says the fence is 12 1/2 m long. Which statement is correct?
options: 12 1/2 m — multiply the wholes and carry the half
28 m — write both over 2, so 7/2 × 8/2 is 56/2
7 1/2 m — join the sections by adding 4 to 3 1/2
questions.explain: Change 3 1/2 to 7/2 before multiplying: 7/2 × 4 = 28/2 = 14 m. The trap is multiplying only the whole number and carrying the 1/2 along — every one of the 4 sections holds a half metre, so 4 halves, a full 2 m, go missing.

questions.question: A raised garden bed at Maya's school measures 2 1/2 m by 1 1/5 m. Every square metre of the bed needs 1/2 of a bag of soil. How many bags of soil are needed?
questions.explain: First the area: 2 1/2 × 1 1/5 = 5/2 × 6/5 = 30/10 = 3 m², then the soil: 3 × 1/2 = 1 1/2 bags. The trap is multiplying the whole numbers and the fraction parts separately, giving an area of 2 1/10 m² instead of 3 m².

questions.question: Priya says: 'Multiplying always makes a number bigger, so 8 × 3/4 has to be more than 8.' Which reply is right?
options: Yes — the answer is 8 3/4, since the 3/4 joins onto 8
Yes — multiplying makes amounts grow, so it is over 8
No — 3/4 of 8 is 6, so taking part of 8 leaves less
questions.explain: Multiplying by a fraction smaller than 1 takes a part of the amount, so 8 × 3/4 = 24/4 = 6, which is less than 8. The trap is believing products always grow — that is only true when the multiplier is bigger than 1.
